front: $R_1$ and $R_2$ are in series across a battery and a capacitor is wired in parallel with $R_2$. What charge does it hold at steady state?
why: Capacitor in parallel with a divider resistor at steady state is a common circuit puzzle

front: A $12$ V battery, a $2$ k$\Omega$ resistor, and an uncharged $10\ \mu$F capacitor sit in series. What is the current the instant the switch closes?
why: Initial RC current calculation is a standard discrete

front: A 12 V battery with internal resistance 1.0 Ω is connected to an external 5.0 Ω resistor. What is the terminal voltage?
why: Terminal voltage V = emf - Ir is a calculation equation

front: A battery of emf $12$ V and internal resistance $0.5\,\Omega$ delivers $4$ A. What is its terminal voltage?
why: Near-restatement of the terminal voltage calculation card

front: A defibrillator must deliver $200$ J from a $100\,\mu$F capacitor. What principle sets the charging voltage?
why: Rearranged restatement of the U = 1/2 CV^2 defibrillator card

front: A defibrillator's $100\ \mu$F capacitor charged to $2000$ V stores $U = \frac12 CV^2 =$ {{c1::$200$ J}}.
why: Capacitor energy U = 1/2 CV^2 is a calculation equation

front: A neuron's membrane time constant is $\tau = R_mC_m$, so a longer $\tau$ produces {{c1::greater temporal summation}} of successive inputs.
why: Membrane time constant is a plausible neuro passage step

front: A voltmeter is placed {{c1::in parallel}} with the element and must have very high resistance.
why: Voltmeter in parallel, high resistance is a stock discrete

front: Adding another parallel branch raises total current, so the internal $Ir$ drop grows and terminal voltage {{c1::falls}}.
why: Internal resistance sag under added load is a second-step application

front: After a long time in a DC circuit, current through a capacitor is:
why: Restates the capacitor wire-then-open card

front: After one time constant, what fraction of its final charge does a charging capacitor hold?
why: 63% after one time constant is commonly asked

front: An ammeter is placed {{c1::in series}} and must have very low resistance so it barely perturbs the circuit.
why: Ammeter in series, low resistance is a stock discrete

front: At steady state a capacitor in series with a resistor passes {{c1::zero}} current, so the full battery voltage sits across the capacitor.
why: Steady-state series RC with Q = CV is a common calculation

front: At the instant an uncharged capacitor is connected, it behaves like:
why: Restates the capacitor wire-then-open card

front: Capacitors in parallel add directly: $C_{eq} = {{c1::C_1 + C_2}}$.
why: Parallel capacitor addition rule is used in calculations every year

front: Capacitors in parallel:
why: Restates the parallel capacitor cloze card

front: Capacitors in series combine like resistors in parallel: $1/C_{eq} = {{c1::1/C_1 + 1/C_2}}$.
why: Series capacitor reciprocal rule is used in calculations every year

front: Doubling $R$ in a charging RC circuit changes what, and what stays the same?
why: RC parameter change reasoning is commonly asked

front: During discharge, capacitor charge decays {{c1::exponentially}}, following $Q = Q_0e^{-t/\tau}$.
why: Exponential discharge form is on the outline

front: EMF is not a force; it is the {{c1::energy per unit charge}} supplied by a source, measured in volts.
why: EMF as energy per charge is commonly tested

front: In a charging RC circuit, when is the current largest?
why: Restates the capacitor-as-wire-at-t=0 card

front: In an RC circuit an uncharged capacitor acts like a {{c1::wire}} at $t = 0$ and like an open switch at steady state.
why: Capacitor as wire at t=0 and open at steady state is asked every year

front: Myelin raises membrane resistance, lengthening the axon's length constant, so a passive signal decays {{c1::less}} with distance.
why: Myelin and length constant is a neuro passage crossover

front: Physically, why does putting capacitors in series lower the total capacitance?
why: Physical picture behind series capacitors; supporting reasoning

front: That $2000$ V defibrillator discharges through a $50\ \Omega$ thorax. Estimate the peak current and the pulse duration.
why: Defibrillator pulse estimate is a passage-style application

front: The RC time constant is $\tau = {{c1::RC}}$ and carries units of seconds.
why: tau = RC is a calculation equation and appears every year

front: Two identical capacitors are connected across the same battery, first in parallel and then in series. Which arrangement stores more energy?
why: Series vs parallel capacitor energy comparison is a common calculation

front: What error appears when a real voltmeter with finite resistance is placed across a large resistor?
why: Meter loading is a plausible experimental passage point

front: When is a battery's terminal voltage greater than its emf?
why: Terminal voltage above emf during charging is secondary

front: Why do car headlights dim when the starter motor engages?
why: Restates the internal-resistance sag card

front: Why do series capacitors carry equal charge while parallel capacitors carry equal voltage?
why: Why series capacitors share charge is supporting reasoning

front: Why is an axon membrane modeled as a resistor and capacitor in parallel?
why: Axon as RC circuit is a neuro passage crossover

front: Why can a worn-out battery read its full EMF on a voltmeter, yet fail as soon as a real load is attached?
why: Open-circuit voltage vs loaded terminal voltage is a standard real-battery question.

front: A voltmeter reads $9.0$ V across an unloaded battery and $8.0$ V once a $4.0\,\Omega$ resistor is connected across it. What is the internal resistance?
why: Extracting internal resistance from two readings is a common discrete calculation.

front: Four $1.5$ V cells are stacked in series, but one is inserted backward. The total EMF is {{c1::$3.0$ V}}.
why: Series cell stacks and the reversed-cell trap appear in circuit questions regularly.

front: Two identical $1.5$ V cells, each with internal resistance $r$, are connected in parallel. What are the pack's EMF and internal resistance?
why: Parallel battery packs are secondary to series stacks on the exam.

front: A phone battery is rated $2000$ mAh at $3.7$ V. How much charge does it hold, and roughly how much energy?
why: Capacity unit conversions show up in passage-based device questions.

front: What happens if an ammeter is mistakenly connected in parallel across a lamp?
why: Misplaced-meter consequences are a classic conceptual circuit question.

front: A voltmeter wired in series with a $100\,\Omega$ resistor across an ideal $9.0$ V battery reads about {{c1::$9.0$ V}}.
why: Misplaced-meter consequences are a classic conceptual circuit question.

front: A battery's EMF is the cell potential of its galvanic cell, set by the redox reaction through $\Delta G = -nFE$; the battery's positive terminal is the {{c1::cathode}}.
why: The electrochemistry bridge is tested, but mostly in the chemistry topic.

front: Capacitance is the charge stored per volt, $C = Q/V$, measured in {{c1::farads}} ($1\text{ F} = 1\text{ C/V}$).
why: C = Q/V underlies every capacitor question on the MCAT.

front: A parallel-plate capacitor's plate area is doubled and its plate gap is tripled. What is the new capacitance?
why: Parallel-plate scaling is tested on nearly every exam.

front: $12$ V is applied across capacitor plates $2.0$ mm apart. What is the electric field between them?
why: $E = V/d$ between plates links capacitors to electrostatics questions.

front: How does a dielectric between the plates raise a capacitor's capacitance?
why: The mechanism of dielectrics is a common conceptual question.

front: A dielectric ($\kappa$) is slid into a capacitor that stays connected to its battery. What happens to $Q$, $V$, $E$, and $U$?
why: Connected-vs-disconnected capacitor changes are tested on every MCAT.

front: A $2.0\,\mu$F capacitor charged to $100$ V is disconnected, then filled with a $\kappa = 4$ slab. What are its new voltage and stored energy?
why: Connected-vs-disconnected capacitor changes are tested on every MCAT.

front: The plates of a charged, isolated capacitor are pulled apart to twice their separation. What happens to $C$, $Q$, $V$, and $U$?
why: Connected-vs-disconnected capacitor changes are tested on every MCAT.

front: With the battery still connected, doubling a capacitor's plate separation {{c1::halves}} both its charge and its stored energy.
why: Connected-vs-disconnected capacitor changes are tested on every MCAT.

front: A capacitor's stored energy is $U = \tfrac{1}{2}QV = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^2 =$ {{c1::$Q^2/2C$}}.
why: Choosing the right energy form drives every capacitor energy question.

front: A battery charges an uncharged capacitor through a resistor, moving charge $Q$ at voltage $V$. How much energy does the battery supply, and where does it all go?
why: The half-lost-as-heat result appears mainly as a passage-level conceptual trap.

front: A $3.0\,\mu$F and a $6.0\,\mu$F capacitor are in series across $12$ V. What voltage does each one take?
why: Voltage division in series capacitors is a common network calculation.

front: When a charged capacitor discharges through a resistor, the current flows in the {{c1::opposite}} direction to the charging current.
why: Charging-vs-discharging behavior is commonly tested with RC graphs.

front: A charging capacitor follows $Q(t) =$ {{c1::$C\varepsilon(1 - e^{-t/RC})$}}, rising quickly and then leveling off.
why: Exact exponential forms are recognition-only, supplied in passages.

front: A $2.0\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor charges a $50\,\mu$F capacitor from a battery. About how long until the capacitor is essentially fully charged?
why: Time-constant arithmetic is secondary, mostly in passage questions.

front: A capacitor reaches half its final charge (or loses half while discharging) after about {{c1::$0.69\tau$}}.
why: The half-time is marked low-yield in the lesson.

front: A toxin opens many extra $\text{K}^+$ leak channels in a neuron. How do the membrane resistance and time constant change?
why: Channel opening as parallel resistors is a common bioelectricity translation.

front: Why does myelin LOWER the axon's membrane capacitance?
why: Myelin as series capacitors is a favorite physics-in-biology question.

front: In a myelinated axon, the action potential is regenerated only at the {{c1::nodes of Ranvier}}, where voltage-gated $\text{Na}^+$ channels are concentrated.
why: Saltatory conduction is tested in both physics and biology contexts.

front: In multiple sclerosis, how do a demyelinated internode's capacitance and resistance compare with a healthy one, and why does conduction suffer?
why: Demyelination is a common clinical framing of membrane RC properties.

front: A defibrillator charges its capacitor over $6.0$ s and delivers the same energy in about $6.0$ ms. How does the delivery power compare with the charging power?
why: Defibrillator energy-and-power reasoning is a common applied capacitor question.
